This is a postmenopausal woman presenting with the classic symptom of endometrial cancer — abnormal uterine (vaginal) bleeding. The endometrial biopsy definitively confirms **Grade 1 endometrioid adenocarcinoma**, the most common and hormonally driven subtype of endometrial cancer, strongly associated with unopposed estrogen exposure (though no explicit risk factors are reported here, endogenous or occult sources remain possible in a postmenopausal woman). Vaginal atrophy is expected in this demographic and does not explain the bleeding; rather, it may have facilitated detection of the abnormal bleeding. The non-tender left adnexal mass is highly concerning: in the context of known endometrial cancer, it raises suspicion for either (a) synchronous primary ovarian cancer (e.g., endometrioid or clear cell carcinoma — which commonly co-occur with endometrial endometrioid adenocarcinoma as part of the Lynch syndrome or sporadic dual primaries), (b) metastatic spread from the endometrium to the ovary (less common for Grade 1 tumors but possible), or (c) benign pathology (e.g., cystadenoma, fibroma) — though malignancy must be ruled out urgently. The thickened endometrial stripe on ultrasound corroborates the biopsy finding.
